No. GM food produces much better yields and is often more resistant to disease or pests. This will have absolutely no effect on the use of GMO crops.

Surprisingly, it's untrue that GM foodstuffs offer improved yields. When you're saying that I assume you think that if for instance I plant one regular unit of corn, and one GM unit of corn the GM unit would end up with a yield of 1.2 while the regular would only end up with a yield of 1. This incorrect.

The increases in yield come from meta-analyses studies that take all before and after study cases without any sort of normalization done to try to ensure you're comparing apples to apples. So Monsanto decides to field test a soy bean in the Philippines. They go and completely support a farmer and update all of his technology, hardware, and so on to modern standards. And they also have him plant the GM seed. His before and after yield is massively improved primarily because of access to better technology, but the seed itself gets all the credit in the meta-analyses.

This is a study comparing genetically engineered yields from foodstuffs in America to yields of normal seed planted in Western Europe over a period of 15 years. The non GM yield of Western Europe was actually slightly higher than that of the GM yield in the United States. The primary benefit of GM seed is related to pesticide/herbicide treatment allowing patented solutions for farmers without access to other means, but modern technology also achieves at least as much without genetic engineering.

This is the most commonly cited meta-analysis that claims a 22% increase in yield from GMO seed. You can see in this graph from the study that the mode (or most common result in a list) of yield change is 0. But the average is brought up to that 22% exclusively by the sort of studies I'm mentioning. Well that and a bit of a selection bias. The majority of these sort of studies are funded by big-business agriculture. There's a strong disincentive against them publishing results that do not support their narrative. For that matter journals themselves are also somewhat reluctant to publish negative results. Not negative as in sounding bad, but negative as in evidence of a 'not'.
